title: The poverty of anti-tech thought
gist: Responding to political scientist Henry Farrell's critique of his review of Acemoglu and Johnson's 'Power and Progress,' Noah Smith argues that equating persuasion with coercive power is tautological and wrong, that Americans embraced Big Tech because they liked the products rather than being tricked into it, and that despite AI backlash currently pushing toward quasi-nationalization of major AI companies, effective-but-flawed operators like Elon Musk should be used rather than rejected wholesale.

themes.theme: Why Americans actually embraced Big Tech

insights.claim: Noah Smith's central argument is that Americans embraced Big Tech products like the iPhone, Amazon, Facebook, and ChatGPT because they genuinely liked the technology itself, not because techno-industrialists persuaded or tricked them into it through a marketplace of ideas.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rejects the premise behind anti-tech regulatory arguments that consumer adoption of Big Tech products was manufactured via persuasion, which matters for how antitrust and AI-regulation debates get framed.
insights.quote: It wasn’t the marketplace of ideas; it was just the marketplace.
insights.locator: The Americans who loved the iPhone

insights.claim: Smith argues Steve Jobs needed no argument beyond the iPhone itself, and Jeff Bezos needed no argument beyond Amazon itself, to win mass consumer adoption.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A product-quality framework investors can apply when evaluating whether a tech company's growth is driven by durable product value versus marketing or lock-in.
insights.quote: The iPhone was the only argument Steve Jobs really needed. Amazon was the only argument Jeff Bezos really needed.
insights.locator: The Americans who loved the iPhone

insights.claim: Smith argues Acemoglu and Johnson's definition of 'power' in Power and Progress — which counts mere successful persuasion alongside coercive acts like slavery and feudal extraction — is a poorly supported conceptual move that muddles distinct phenomena rather than yielding insight or policy solutions.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A critique of the intellectual foundation behind the 'techbros have illegitimate power' narrative that underlies calls for breaking up or heavily regulating tech companies.
insights.quote: I do not understand why we should put accidental success in a nonviolent marketplace of ideas in the same conceptual category as chattel slavery and feudalism.
insights.locator: In fact, I have to confess

insights.claim: Smith argues Henry Farrell's claim that Smith himself has 'power' because people like his arguments (and that people like his arguments because he has power) is a tautological, unfalsifiable definition under which a powerless person could never convince anyone of anything.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Illustrates a specific logical flaw investors should watch for in 'social influence equals power' arguments used to justify regulating persuasive but non-coercive market actors.
insights.quote: Why does Noah have power? Because people like his arguments! And why do people like his arguments? Because he has power!
insights.locator: What bothers me about this definition

insights.claim: Smith concedes that when rich people or companies use money to broadcast ideas more loudly than others can afford to (e.g., a billboard campaign), that is a legitimate concern distinct from persuasion itself, and that Acemoglu and Johnson would have been on firmer ground if they had stuck to that narrower claim.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Draws a clearer, more defensible line for tech-money-in-politics concerns: spending power to amplify a message is worth scrutinizing, but organic persuasive success is not the same problem.
insights.quote: It’s silver, rather than silver tongues, that’s doing the work.

themes.theme: Origins and scope of the elite anti-tech turn

insights.claim: New York Times coverage of Facebook shifted sharply more negative after the 2016 election, coinciding with the narrative that Facebook 'fake news' disinformation swung the election to Trump — a key trigger for the broader elite-left turn against tech.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Dates and identifies the specific media-narrative inflection point (2016 'fake news') that reshaped elite discourse toward Big Tech, useful context for the origin of ongoing tech-regulation political pressure.
insights.locator: An easy way to see the shift in sentiment

insights.claim: Beyond the 2016 trigger, the left-tech breakup was driven by internal progressive-values conflicts within tech companies, anger over tech-driven rent increases in major cities, technocapitalists increasingly entering policy through philanthropy and clashing with existing players, and resentment from rising inequality among educated classes.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Provides a multi-factor causal model (culture conflicts, rents, philanthropy-driven policy influence, inequality resentment) for understanding the durability and breadth of elite anti-tech sentiment beyond a single 2016 event.
insights.locator: 2016 was a trigger, but it wasn't the sole cause

insights.claim: The New Brandeis antitrust movement explicitly framed breaking up Big Tech companies as protecting democracy from political power rather than protecting consumers from higher prices, but this legal theory won few court victories because US antitrust law doesn't allow breakups for political reasons.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Explains why democracy-framed antitrust theories against Big Tech have largely failed in US courts, a relevant legal-risk data point for tech companies facing antitrust scrutiny.
insights.quote: This approach didn’t win many victories against Big Tech in court — U.S. antitrust law doesn’t leave any room for breaking companies up for political reasons.
insights.locator: The 2010s also saw the rise of the new antitrust movement

insights.claim: The turn against Big Tech has been mostly an elite intellectual phenomenon rather than a mass one: general Democratic-voter sentiment toward tech companies remains broadly positive and hasn't changed much over the years, with Elon Musk as the major exception due to his Trump support and DOGE activities.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests anti-Big-Tech policy pressure is concentrated among policy elites rather than broad voter sentiment, meaning regulatory momentum may not translate into a durable mass political mandate outside the Musk-specific case.
insights.quote: the turn against Big Tech has been mostly an elite phenomenon; Democrats’ sentiment toward tech companies remains broadly positive, and hasn’t changed much over the years.
insights.locator: It's worth noting that the turn against Big Tech

themes.theme: Elon Musk as the effective-but-flawed operator case study

insights.claim: Smith describes Elon Musk as a cruel and selfish man who supported some of America's worst politicians and made the terrible, immoral decision to dismantle USAID, yet credits him as an almost preternaturally effective entrepreneur — the only person to make electric vehicles commercially viable at scale (where GM and Ford failed for decades), the only one to build a company that out-launched China and NASA combined, and currently the only one capable of building the semiconductor fabs America needs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A direct, named assessment that Tesla and SpaceX's execution edge over legacy competitors (GM, Ford, NASA) is attributable specifically to Musk's individual entrepreneurial ability, relevant to competitive-moat analysis in EVs, space launch, and semiconductor fabs.
insights.quote: Elon Musk, I believe, is not a good man. He is a cruel and selfish man.
insights.locator: Elon Musk, I believe, is not a good man

insights.claim: Smith's normative conclusion is that the right approach to an operator like Musk is to utilize his talents as best as possible while working to prevent him from subverting the national interest, rather than rejecting the entire techbro class as parasitic.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames a pragmatic policy stance toward high-impact, ethically flawed founders that argues against blanket regulatory hostility, relevant to how governments might engage with dominant tech founders going forward.
insights.quote: The only thing that makes sense is to utilize his talents as best you can, and do your best to prevent him from subverting the national interest along the way.
insights.locator: What do you do with a man like that?

insights.claim: Smith argues that in most eras societies don't need to worship titans of industry like Steve Jobs, but in every era they need them, and that the left errs by imagining companies like Apple and Amazon could have been built just as well by anonymous organization men rather than specific entrepreneurs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A general thesis on the irreplaceability of specific founder talent that pushes back on narratives discounting individual entrepreneurs' contribution to company success.
insights.quote: Only in a few eras do we decide to worship titans of industry like Steve Jobs. But in every era, we need them.

themes.theme: Where the AI backlash is headed

insights.claim: Smith predicts that popular fear of AI and its data centers is producing a grassroots democratic backlash against the AI industry that no amount of Big Tech money or pro-tech advocacy will stop, and that the government will likely end up quasi-nationalizing the major AI companies in some form to ensure the technology serves the national interest.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete, high-conviction prediction of eventual US government quasi-nationalization of leading AI companies — a material regulatory-risk scenario for investors holding AI-lab-adjacent exposure.
insights.quote: the government will probably end up quasi-nationalizing the big AI companies in some way, in order to ensure that this powerful technology serves the interest of the nation.

insights.claim: Smith frames two possible paths after AI-driven backlash triggers government intervention: a New Deal-style path that incorporates both technology and technologists into a unified drive for national prosperity and security, or a collapse into zero-sum status battles and petty class resentment that leaves nothing accomplished — and argues the current anti-tech movement is steering the country toward the latter.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sets out two distinct AI-policy regime scenarios (integrative New Deal model vs. gridlocked status-conflict model) worth tracking as the actual policy path emerges, with direct implications for AI-sector regulatory risk.
insights.quote: We could emulate the New Deal, and incorporate both technology and technologists into a unified drive for national prosperity and security. Or we could collapse into zero-sum status battles and petty class resentments
insights.locator: We could emulate the New Deal
